Monday. Harsha had to pack his toys for Nani's house. He put the red car in first, because it was fastest. Then he saw his kite and ran to the window with it. The bag stayed empty.
Wednesday. His big sister Ankita drew three pictures on a card: car, blocks, teddy. "One, two, three," she said. Harsha packed the car. He packed the blocks. Then the cat came in, and he chased the cat.
Saturday. Harsha held the card and packed car, blocks, teddy. He clapped. Then he unpacked the teddy to hug it.

qa.q: What did Ankita draw on the card?
qa.a: Car, blocks, teddy.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when he finished packing on Saturday?
qa.a: Harsha felt happy and proud, clapping after packing all three.

qa.q: What helped Harsha keep an order, even for a little while?
qa.a: Ankita's picture card showed one, two, three, so Harsha had a simple order to follow when something shinier appeared.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel watching Harsha chase the cat on Wednesday?
qa.a: Ankita might feel amused and a little impatient, since the plan changed as soon as the cat came in.

grounding: Shows a young child choosing what to pack first by what is fun, and changing the plan whenever something shinier appears.

passage:
On Friday evening in Kodi, near the sea, Shreya dropped her school bag on the verandah. The temple fair had come to the village. "Homework after," she called to her mother, and ran with her friend Ritu to see the giant wheel and the bangle stalls.
She meant it. There was the whole evening.
They came back at eight, sticky with sugar cane juice. Shreya opened her Kannada notebook: one page of writing and ten maths sums. At half past eight, the power went off. Her mother lit one lamp, and the light was too weak for her to see the sums clearly.
She finished at ten, eyes aching, half the sums crossed out. On Monday, her teacher circled four mistakes.
The next Friday, the fair was still there. Shreya sat on the verandah steps and did the sums first, while Ritu waited, grumbling, for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What homework did Shreya have?
qa.a: One page of writing and ten maths sums.

qa.q: How might Shreya have felt doing sums by the weak lamp?
qa.a: Shreya probably felt tired and frustrated, eyes aching and crossing out sums late at night.

qa.q: What did Shreya change the next Friday, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She did the sums first, before the fair, because the bad evening showed that there was not always time later.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel waiting the next Friday?
qa.a: Ritu felt impatient, grumbling while waiting twenty minutes for Shreya to finish.

grounding: Illustrates a child who plays first, sure there will be time, until a bad evening teaches her to do the hard task first.

"Saurabh, how's the physics revision going?"
"Going, Rashmi didi. I'll start in ten minutes."
"You said that at four."
"I had to reply to the class group. Someone asked about the tuition timing."
"And after that?"
"Mummy asked me to get milk. Then my bike chain came off, so I fixed it. Then the cricket group was arguing about Sunday's match…"
"And physics?"
"Physics is… open." He pointed at the book on the bed.
"Saurabh, the exam is in nine days. How many chapters are left?"
"Six."
"Every one of those messages felt urgent, right?"
"Yes! People were waiting."
"Nobody's waiting on physics. It doesn't ping. That's why it keeps sliding."
He looked at his phone. It buzzed again. He turned it face down.
"Okay. Phone in the kitchen for an hour?"
"I'll hold it hostage," she said, holding out her hand. He gave it to her.

qa.q: How many chapters of physics are left?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel about all the messages and small jobs?
qa.a: Saurabh felt they were urgent and productive, as if people were waiting on him, even while physics slid.

qa.q: What small step helped Saurabh get to the important task?
qa.a: Putting his phone in the kitchen with Rashmi didi for an hour, so the loud urgent things could not interrupt.

qa.q: How does Rashmi didi see Saurabh's afternoon?
qa.a: Rashmi didi sees that the quiet, important revision keeps losing to noisy small things, and she steps in with humour to help.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose messages and small chores feel urgent while exam revision keeps sliding.

passage:
Monday. Darshan wrote everything on one sticky note: two assignments, aptitude practice for placements, his grandmother's call, a friend's birthday, the college fest meeting. All starred. He started the assignment, then switched to aptitude, then answered the fest group.
Wednesday. At midnight, nothing was finished. The assignment was half done, the aptitude test half done, and he had forgotten his grandmother's call. He felt like he was failing at everything at once.
Saturday. His classmate Ankita sat with him in the canteen. "Rank them. One to six. And something has to be last."
Darshan argued for twenty minutes. Then he wrote: assignment due Monday first, aptitude second, Grandma on Sunday morning. The fest meeting he would skip, and he messaged the group to say so. It felt terrible for about an hour.
By Sunday night, the assignment was submitted. It was the first thing he had finished in a week.

qa.q: What did Darshan decide to skip?
qa.a: The fest meeting.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel on Wednesday at midnight?
qa.a: Darshan felt overwhelmed and defeated, as if he was failing at everything at once.

qa.q: Why did ranking the tasks help, even though something was left out?
qa.a: Ranking let Darshan focus on the assignment first and finish it, accepting that the fest meeting would be left undone.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt as Darshan argued for twenty minutes?
qa.a: Ankita was probably patient but firm, sure that something had to be last for anything to get done.

grounding: Illustrates a college student who treats every task as top priority until ranking them, and leaving one undone, lets him finish something.

subtype: Saying no to protect the main goal [Actor]
passage:
Subject: Re: Diwali quiz for the floor

Hi Deepak,
Thank you for thinking of me for the Diwali quiz. I really enjoyed doing it last year, and I know the team loves it.
I have to say no this year. The client audit report is due on the 28th, and I'm the only one who has the full data. If I spend evenings on quiz questions, I'll be rushing the audit, and I can't afford mistakes there.
I feel a bit bad saying this, honestly. It's the fun part of the year, and it's easy to help with.
What I can do: I'll send you last year's question file today, so whoever takes it on has a head start. And after the 28th, I'm happy to help with the Christmas lunch.
Sorry, and thank you for understanding.
Chetan

qa.q: When is the client audit report due?
qa.a: The client audit report is due on the 28th.

qa.q: How does Chetan feel about saying no?
qa.a: Chetan feels a bit guilty and awkward, since the quiz is fun and easy to help with.

qa.q: What makes Chetan's no both firm and kind?
qa.a: Chetan gives the real reason, protects the audit time, offers last year's file and suggests help after the deadline.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel reading the email?
qa.a: Deepak might feel a little disappointed but understanding, and helped by getting last year's question file.

grounding: Shows a young professional who declines a fun, low-value request to protect time for a deadline-critical report, despite feeling guilty.

passage:
Yogesh, you're always telling me your to-do list is two pages long. Let me, your Vishal chacha, tell you how I survived my first year running the trucks.
I had four trucks, six drivers and one phone. Every day, forty small fires. I'd make long lists at night and wake up feeling guilty because I never finished half.
An old transporter in Nagpur, Bhatia-ji, laughed at my list. "On Sunday night, write three things. Only three. What must be true by Saturday?"
So I did. One week it was: get the insurance renewed, collect the pending payment from the mill, fix truck two's brakes. Every evening I looked at those three lines. If I'd moved them forward, I slept. The other forty fires still came, but I handled them around the three.
By the end of that year, I had six trucks.
The long list is only guilt, beta. Three things, and look at them every evening.

qa.q: How many trucks did Vishal have at first?
qa.a: I had four trucks.

qa.q: How did young Vishal feel after making long lists at night?
qa.a: Vishal woke up feeling guilty, because he never finished even half of the long lists.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed how Vishal managed his week?
qa.a: Following Bhatia-ji's advice to write only three must-do outcomes each Sunday and check them every evening.

qa.q: How might Bhatia-ji have felt seeing young Vishal's two-page list?
qa.a: Bhatia-ji seemed amused but kind, laughing at the list and offering simpler advice.

grounding: An elder recalls replacing long guilty to-do lists with three weekly outcomes checked every evening.

subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]
passage:
"Avni, why are you lying under the table?"
"Because of the worksheet, Manjula aunty."
"What worksheet?"
"Thirty sums. Thirty! It'll take forever."
"Show me."
Avni crawled out and held up the paper. Three columns of sums, top to bottom.
"Hmm. That's a lot of sums."
"It's impossible."
Manjula aunty took a pencil and drew a line under the fifth sum. "How about just these five?"
"Only five?"
"Only five. Then you can go back under the table if you want."
Avni sat down. She did the first sum. Then the second. "These are easy ones."
"Are they?"
She finished the five and looked up. "Can you draw the next line?"
Manjula aunty drew another line after sum ten.
By dinner, Avni had done twenty. "The last ten tomorrow," she said, and went under the table anyway, grinning.

qa.q: How many sums were on Avni's worksheet?
qa.a: Thirty sums.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when she first looked at the worksheet?
qa.a: Avni felt overwhelmed and stuck, sure the thirty sums were impossible, so she hid under the table.

qa.q: What did Manjula aunty do that made the task possible?
qa.a: Manjula aunty drew a line after five sums, giving Avni a small first piece she could see and finish.

qa.q: How might Manjula aunty feel when Avni asks for the next line?
qa.a: Manjula aunty would probably feel pleased and quietly amused that the small pieces worked.

grounding: Illustrates a child who sees only the size of a thirty-sum worksheet and freezes, until a first small piece makes it doable.

passage:
Tuesday night.
My plan for tonight said "Revise history." That's it. I sat at the desk at seven with the textbook, the notebook and my water bottle, and I just… sat. Where do you even start with "history"? The whole book? The Mughals? The maps?
By eight I had sharpened three pencils and rearranged my shelf.
Ramesh bhaiya came in to borrow the charger and saw my face. "What are you revising?"
"History."
"What's the first thing your hand will actually do?"
I didn't know what he meant. He said, "Not 'revise.' Like, 'read pages 40 to 44 and write five dates on a card.'"
So I wrote exactly that. And I did it, in twenty-five minutes. Then I wrote the next one: "Label the six places on the map on page 46." Did that too.
I'm Madhuri, and I've been writing "study more" for two years. Tomorrow's plan will have a page number in it.

qa.q: Which pages did Ramesh bhaiya suggest reading?
qa.a: Pages 40 to 44.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel sitting at the desk from seven to eight?
qa.a: Madhuri felt stuck and lost, not knowing where to start, so pencils got sharpened instead.

qa.q: What made Madhuri's second plan work?
qa.a: It named a physical first action with page numbers and a small output, like writing five dates on a card, which gave the mind something to grip.

qa.q: How might Ramesh bhaiya feel if he saw tomorrow's plan?
qa.a: Ramesh bhaiya would probably feel pleased and a bit proud that his small tip changed how Madhuri plans.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager whose vague goal of revising history leaves her stuck, until a concrete first step with page numbers gets her moving.

passage:
"Yamini, you've been at that laptop since lunch. How's the essay?"
"Look, Sabina!" Yamini turned the screen. "A timeline. Research in green, outline in blue, drafts in purple. Every day till the deadline, in fifteen-minute slots."
"It's beautiful. How many words have you written?"
"Of the essay? Well… none yet. But the plan's ready."
"You said the plan was ready yesterday."
"Yesterday I didn't have the colours."
Sabina sat on the bed. "What's the first sentence going to be about?"
Yamini went quiet. "That's the problem. It's about why I want the scholarship. And every time I start, it sounds stupid."
"So the timeline is safer."
"…Maybe."
"Close the timeline. Write one bad sentence about why you want it. Just one. I'll wait."
Yamini opened a blank page. Her fingers hovered. She typed: "I want this because my mother never got to study." She stared at it.
"That's not stupid," Sabina said softly.

qa.q: How many words of the essay had Yamini written?
qa.a: None yet.

qa.q: Why did Yamini keep working on the timeline instead of the essay?
qa.a: Yamini was afraid the first sentence would sound stupid, so planning felt safer than starting.

qa.q: What did Sabina suggest, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sabina suggested closing the timeline and writing one bad sentence, which made the frightening first step small enough to take.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel reading Yamini's first sentence?
qa.a: Sabina felt moved and gentle, telling Yamini softly that it was not stupid.

grounding: Shows a student who builds a colour-coded plan to avoid the frightening first sentence of an essay, until a friend helps her start.

subtype: Splitting a project into checkable pieces [Response]
passage:
"Gurpreet, how are you so calm? The fest budget file is due Friday and I'm panicking for you," Preeti said.
"Because it isn't one job. It's eleven small ones." Gurpreet turned the notebook around. Eleven lines, some ticked.
"Collect quotes from the sound vendor. Tick. Enter food costs. Tick. Check last year's decoration bills…"
"Each of these is under an hour?"
"Every single one. If something takes longer, I split it again. 'Make the budget' is scary. 'Enter the food costs' is just boring."
"And the ticks?"
"That's the best part. By Wednesday I've ticked seven. I can see I'm getting there. When I look at the whole file, I get the same dread you're feeling. When I look at the next line, I don't."
Preeti pulled out her own notebook. "My project report. Can you help me break it up?"
"First line: open the report and write the headings. Twenty minutes. Go."

qa.q: How many small jobs did Gurpreet split the budget file into?
qa.a: It's eleven small ones.

qa.q: Why does Gurpreet feel calm about the Friday deadline?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels calm and steady because the file is split into eleven small jobs, and the ticks show real progress.

qa.q: Why does Gurpreet's method lower the dread?
qa.a: Each piece takes under an hour and gets ticked, so there is real evidence of progress and the next step feels boring rather than scary.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel after writing the headings?
qa.a: Preeti would likely feel relieved and a little hopeful, having finished one clear piece of a report that seemed huge.

grounding: Illustrates a student who splits a large budget task into pieces under an hour and ticks them off, lowering the dread of the whole.
